title: The Cure of Imperfect Sight by Treatment Without Glasses (Perfect Sight Without Glasses)
author: William H. Bates
edition_cited: New York: Central Fixation Publishing Co., 1920; University of Toronto scan, archive.org cureofimperfects00bateuoft
locator_hints: Chapter XII 'Palming' (printed pp. 123 ff.): lights and colours seen when palming, ways to reach black
Chapter XIII 'Memory as an aid to vision'
Chapter XI 'The Use of Strong Lights' / chapter on the sun (c. printed pp. 119, 177-189): looking at the sun, sun-glass on the eye
Chapter on illusions of imperfect and of normal sight (floating specks, colour of the sun, twinkling stars)
summary: The inverse case. Bates teaches 'palming': closing the eyes and covering them with the palms to exclude all light, with the goal of seeing a perfect black. He reports that most patients instead see illusions of lights and colours, from imperfect black to kaleidoscopic appearances so vivid they seem actually seen, and treats these as a sign of strain to be removed. He gives troubleshooting for people who cannot get black (remembering a black object, shifting, swinging, noting that fatigue, hunger and worry increase the lights). Other chapters recommend exposing the eyes to strong light and looking at the sun, and discuss after-effects such as blind spots and coloured suns.
why_relevant: A detailed public-domain account of closed-eye lights arising under sense closure, with a method and troubleshooting aimed at abolishing them: useful as a counter-instruction and as testimony about what conditions produce the lights. Also an early source for sun-gazing advice.

date_evidence.basis: archive.org metadata for cureofimperfects00bateuoft gives 1920; first edition

notes: Safety: the sun-gazing advice is medically dangerous (solar retinopathy); set sun_gazing. Palming is light covering, not pressure on the eyeball. Bates's physiological theory is rejected by ophthalmology; the observations about closed-eye lights are what matters here.
